name: Honestus
bio: Honestus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 66, 274).

poems.title: Book VII, 66: On the Same
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: The staff, and wallet, and thick cloak, were the very light burden of wise Diogenes in life. I bring all to the ferryman, for I left nothing on earth. But you, Cerberus dog, fawn on me, the Dog.

poems.title: Book VII, 274
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: T announce the name of Timocles and look round in every direction over the salt sea, wondering where his corpse may be. Alas the fishes have devoured him ere this, and I, this useless stone, bear this idle writing carved on me.

poems.title: Book IX, 216
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: You will cite the holy marriage of Harmonia, but that of Oedipus was unlawful. You will tell me of Antigone’s piety, but her brothers were most wicked. Ino was made immortal, but Athamas was ill-fated. The lyre built the walls by its music, but the strains of the flute were fatal to them. So did Heaven compound the destiny of Thebes, mixing good and evil in equal portions.

poems.title: Book IX, 225
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: Asopis fount and Pegasis are sister springs, the one a:river-god’s gift, the other a horse’s, both gushing forth at a blow of the foot. The horse cut the veins of Helicon, the river those of Acrocorinth. How equally happy the heel’s aim in each case !

poems.title: Book IX, 230
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: Thou wert sore tired by the ascent of great Helicon, but didst drink thy fill of the sweet waters of the spring of Pegasus. Even so the labour of study is up-hill, but if thou attainest the summit thou shalt quaff the pleasant gift of the Muses.

poems.title: Book IX, 250
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: I, Thebes, rose at the sound of the lyre, and sunk in ruins at that of the flute. Alas for the Muse that was adverse to harmony! They now lie deaf, the remains of my towers, once charmed by the lyre, the stones that took their places of their own accord in the muse-built walls, a gift that cost thee, Amphion, no labour; for with thy seven-stringed lyre thou didst build thy seven-gated city.

poems.title: Book IX, 292
poems.author: Honestus
poems.text: Aristion was burning the corpse of one son when she heard the other was shipwrecked. A double grief consumed a single heart. Alas! Fate divided this mother in two, since she gave one child to fire and the other to cruel water.
